context: The two-level organization is the field's current working architecture, and its models account for specific observations beyond the deletions that motivated the split: the genetically identified interneuron classes mapped onto the model \citep{rybak_organization_2015} and the organization of circuits controlling two-joint muscles \citep{shevtsova_modeling_2016}, a convergence problem a robot muscle routed across two joints also presents. Coupling such circuits to musculoskeletal models shows how afferent feedback shapes CPG output \citep{markin_afferent_2010} and how biomechanics and sensory feedback regularize the behavior of different CPG architectures \citep{deng_biomechanical_2022}. Physiologically plausible models of human locomotion use the same machinery to dissect the relative contributions of reflexes and CPGs, with locomotor primitives, Ia, II, and Ib pathways, and Renshaw cells represented explicitly \citep{dirusso_investigating_2023}, and recent models address interlimb coordination under abrupt perturbations such as the sudden loss of ground support \citep{shinohara_mechanisms_2025}. How this architecture is expressed as simulable circuit models is the subject of Section~\ref{sec:bg_compneuro}; the locomotor controller developed in Chapter~\ref{ch:sns} is built directly on this two-level organization.

context: Neuromechanical simulation, the coupling of a musculoskeletal model to a model of the neural controller that drives it, has advanced along three partially overlapping lines. The first line embeds reflex physiology directly into the controller. The muscle-reflex walking model of \citet{geyer_musclereflex_2010} demonstrated that positive force, length, and velocity feedback around each muscle, organized with simple interlimb coordination, is sufficient to produce self-stabilizing human-like walking dynamics and realistic muscle activations without any central pattern generator. That model became the reference point for a generation of reflex-based neuromechanical controllers, including the cat hindlimb models of Section~\ref{sec:bg_compneuro} \citep{markin_afferent_2010, shevtsova_modeling_2016} and their extensions. Hybrid work makes the complementarity of the two strategies explicit: \citet{haeufle_benefit_2018} combined feed-forward muscle activations with neuronal reflex feedback in simulated human walking and found that the robustness benefit of each depends on which muscle carries it.

section: 2.10 Testing Neuromechanical Hypotheses on Robots: The Ethical Case
anchor_status: Current review start mapped to frozen source; highlight end unavailable
highlight: Not exposed by current review UI; source line below is context, not an exact highlight.
context: The experiments this research program is designed to enable, including deleting a muscle from a limb, blocking a sensory pathway, lesioning part of a rhythm generator, and applying tonic stimulation to spinal circuits, cannot be performed on healthy humans. Invasive intervention on the human neuromuscular system is limited to clinical populations, is tightly constrained by ethics review, and permits neither the within-subject control nor the reversibility that neuromechanical hypotheses demand. The same experiments in animals also carry real moral cost, and their justification is governed by the Three Rs framework: replacement of animal subjects with non-animal methods, reduction of the numbers required, and refinement of the remaining procedures \citep{russell_principles_1959, tannenbaum_russell_2015}. A robot that implements a validated neuromechanical hypothesis is precisely such a replacement method: every deletion, lesion, and stimulation experiment that runs on the synthetic nervous system is an experiment that does not require a living subject, and the robot population can be duplicated exactly, so that ``subjects'' are statistically identical across conditions, an experimental repeatability no breeding colony can offer. The failure modes of these experiments damage hardware, not tissue.

context: Existing software supplied separate parts of the solution. OpenSim supplied musculoskeletal geometry, MyoConverter translated it to MuJoCo, and SNS-Toolbox supplied neuron and synapse models \citep{delp_opensim_2007, caggiano_myosuite_2022, todorov_mujoco_2012, nourse_sns_2023}. The MuJoCo version used here supports scripted simulation and parameter searches but uses rigid tendons; its Python interface does not provide the block-based circuit assembly needed for this workflow. Simulink supplies that graphical construction, while Simscape Multibody imports mechanical geometry, including SolidWorks-derived mechanisms. AnimatLab retains the reference controllers but is unsupported, relies on an older physics engine, and ran these simulations slowly. The tools connect these complementary environments and use matched tests to check what transfers between them.

highlight: Historical exact highlight (22 Oct. capture): Two definitions cover most of the neuroscience vocabulary used below. First, the locomotor controller is a two-level central pattern generator: a rhythm generator sets the timing of the step cycle, and a pattern-formation layer shapes that timing into phase-appropriate activation of antagonist muscle groups \citep{rybak_modelling_2006}. Each leg's rhythm generator is a pair of mutually inhibiting antagonist populations, one extensor and one flexor, so that only one is strongly active at a time. Second, in the non-spiking (graded) formulation used for most of this work, each neuron is electrically a nonlinear RC circuit: synaptic current charges a membrane capacitance through a leak conductance, and the resulting membrane voltage, tens of millivolts, is both the neuron's state and its output \citep{nourse_sns_2023}. Graded chemical synapses couple these units: a depolarized presynaptic cell opens a conductance in the postsynaptic membrane whose sign makes the connection excitatory or inhibitory. The sensory channels that close the loop are the muscle afferents, Ia signaling muscle length and velocity, Ib signaling muscle force, and group II signaling length, together with heel and toe contact sensors.
